Token: The smallest unit of text a model works with — often a whole word, but sometimes a syllable, punctuation mark, or word fragment. Models read and write in tokens, not characters.
Tokenisation: Splitting input text into tokens before the model can process it. A standardisation step that happens before any real understanding takes place.
Embedding: Mapping a token to a point in a high-dimensional mathematical space where meaning is encoded as position. Words with similar meanings end up close together, which is how a model 'knows' that dog and cat are more related than dog and bicycle.
Vector: An ordered list of numbers representing a token, word, or document as coordinates in embedding space. Similar meanings produce vectors that sit near each other.
Semantic search: Finding text by meaning rather than exact keywords, by comparing the embedding of a query against the embeddings of stored passages and returning the closest matches.
Neural network: The layered mathematical structure an LLM is built from. Input flows through layer after layer, each building a richer representation — early layers catch basic patterns, deeper layers grasp context and intent.
Transformer: The neural-network architecture behind modern LLMs. It stacks attention and feed-forward layers; an encoder processes the input sequence and a decoder generates output. GPT-style models are decoder-only.
Attention: The mechanism that lets a transformer link words that are far apart in a sentence, deciding which parts of the input are most relevant to each other when forming a response.
Generation: Producing output one token at a time. The model predicts the single most probable next token, appends it, and repeats — which is why LLMs can feel like they are 'thinking out loud'.
Inference: Running a trained model to produce output for new input. No learning happens at inference time — the model's weights are fixed; it only applies what it already learned.
LLM: Large Language Model — a neural network trained on vast amounts of text that learns patterns in language (grammar, facts, reasoning styles) and generates responses based on those learned patterns rather than looking things up.
GenAI: Generative AI — systems built around a large language model that produce new content (text, code, structured data) in response to a prompt and surrounding context.
Prompt: The input you give a model. In practice it is assembled into a fuller prompt context before generation begins.
Prompt context: Everything the model sees before it generates: the system prompt, the user's message, any retrieved documents, and any earlier tool results. Richer, more relevant context produces better output.
System prompt: Instructions that define how the model should behave — its persona, rules, and constraints. Sent in the system role, ahead of the user's message.
Role: A label on each message that tells the model what to treat as instructions, what to answer, and what is prior conversation. The three roles are system (persona and rules), user (input), and assistant (previous model responses).
RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation — keeping the base model frozen but supplying relevant context at inference time. The system embeds the question and a corpus, retrieves the most similar passages, and adds them to the prompt so the model can answer from your own data.
Knowledge source: An external database or document store a GenAI system searches (via RAG) to extend what the model knows beyond its training data.
Context window: The maximum number of tokens (system prompt + history + retrieved context + question) a model can attend to at once. When it fills, the oldest tokens drop out and the model loses access to them — large workflows split work into stages or use RAG to stay under the cap.
Temperature: A sampling control over randomness. Low values make output more deterministic and repeatable; higher values make it more varied and creative. Docs-grounded answers usually use a low temperature.
Greedy decoding: A sampling strategy that always picks the highest-probability next token. Deterministic and repeatable, but can be repetitive.
Top-k sampling: Restricting the next-token choice to the k most likely candidates, then sampling among them — a way to add controlled variety without picking implausible tokens.
Top-p sampling: Also called nucleus sampling. The next token is sampled from the smallest set of candidates whose combined probability exceeds p, adapting how many options are considered to the model's confidence.
Hallucination: When a model produces fluent but factually wrong or fabricated output. Grounding answers with RAG and citing sources reduces it.
Ollama: A tool for running open LLMs locally via a simple HTTP API (default http://localhost:11434). In this course PDI calls Ollama so model inference stays on the VM and nothing leaves the box.
PDI: Pentaho Data Integration — the ETL platform used throughout this course as the orchestration layer that assembles inputs, calls the model, parses the response, and writes typed results back out.
Spoon: The desktop design tool for building and running PDI transformations and jobs.
Transformation: A PDI data-flow made of steps connected by hops, defined in a .ktr file. It moves and reshapes rows of data — including calling an LLM mid-flow.
Job: A PDI orchestration unit (.kjb) that sequences transformations and other tasks, handling control flow, conditions, and error paths.
Orchestration: PDI's role as the conductor: it gathers structured and unstructured inputs, hands them to the model with the right prompt, parses what comes back, and writes typed results to databases, files, or APIs.
Sentiment analysis: Classifying the emotional tone of text — positive, negative, or neutral — for example to score customer reviews. A common LLM-enrichment use case in PDI.
Named Entity Recognition: Extracting named things from free text — people, organisations, places, dates — into structured fields. Handles reworded and paraphrased mentions that brittle regex rules would miss.
Data enrichment: Filling gaps the source data can't, by deriving new fields from free text — classification, language detection, intent labelling, country inference — using a model that understands meaning.
Data quality: Using a model to detect, flag, or correct problems in data — typos, inconsistencies, mis-categorisations — that rule-based checks struggle to catch.
Summarisation: Condensing long text into a short, faithful summary as a pipeline step, so downstream stages or humans work with the gist instead of the full document.
Multi-stage pipeline: Decomposing a complex task into focused stages, each with a tight prompt. Errors are easier to localise and you can mix model sizes — a cheap classifier feeding an expensive synthesiser.
LangExtract: A lightweight approach (here, a REST service backed by Ollama) for turning free-form text into structured rows when regex is too brittle and full model training is too heavy.
Structured extraction: Pulling typed, schema-shaped fields out of unstructured text — support tickets, clinical notes, contracts — so the rest of an ETL flow can join, aggregate, and store them.
Schema: The declared shape of the data you want back — the fields and types an extraction service should produce. Centralising the schema in one service means upgrades roll out everywhere at once.
Agent: A system that reasons over intermediate output in a loop — calling the model, inspecting the result, fetching more data or calling a tool, then calling the model again — until it converges on an answer. A loop, not a single function call.
Agentic: Describing behaviour where the model can decide to act — call an API, run code, search — and feed the result back into its context to form its final answer.
Tool calling: Giving a model the ability to invoke external functions or APIs during a conversation. The result returns into the context and shapes the model's next step.
Agent-as-a-Service: Wrapping an agent behind a service endpoint so PDI stays the orchestrator and many pipelines can call the same agent. Model swaps, prompt tweaks, and tool additions roll out once at the service.
Confidence threshold: A routing rule that trusts the model's answer when its certainty is high and escalates to a human (or a fallback) when it is low — scaling automation without sacrificing quality on edge cases.
Base64: A text encoding that represents binary data (such as an image) as ASCII characters, so it can be embedded in JSON payloads sent to or from a model API.
